summary: This informational document describes ways to support multicast listeners in Proxy Mobile IPv6 domains without changing the mobility or multicast standards. The Local Mobility Anchor acts as the multicast anchor, and Mobile Access Gateways handle listener signaling. It shows how to deploy existing parts together.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6224 describes how a Proxy Mobile IPv6 network can deliver multicast data to listeners after they move to a new access gateway. The network's gateways and mobility anchors handle the subscription signaling; the mobile node does not need mobility-specific multicast behavior.

questions: how do mobile nodes receive multicast in pmipv6
how does multicast work in proxy mobile ipv6
subtitle: How a Proxy Mobile IPv6 network can keep multicast subscriptions working as listeners move.

tldr.problem: Proxy Mobile IPv6 manages a mobile node's movement in the network, but it does not define how multicast subscriptions follow the node between access gateways.
tldr.mechanism: Mobile Access Gateways run MLD proxy functions, aggregate listener reports, and send them through tunnels to Local Mobility Anchors, which anchor multicast subscriptions.
tldr.outcome: The deployment approach supports multicast listeners without changing the mobility or multicast protocol standards. Mobile multicast senders are outside the document's scope.

facts.label: Listener signaling
facts.value: MLD for IPv6; IGMP for IPv4

today: RFC 6224 is an Informational RFC published in April 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it describes a deployment approach using PMIPv6, MLD, and IGMP functions.

sections.title: Multicast in Proxy Mobile IPv6
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) lets the network manage a mobile node's IP mobility without requiring the node to participate in mobility signaling. The Mobile Access Gateway (MAG) and Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) perform that work.

Multicast requires additional listener membership handling. RFC 6224 describes a deployment that uses existing mobility and multicast functions: MAGs provide Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) proxy behavior, and LMAs act as multicast subscription anchors. It does not cover mobile multicast senders.
sections.plainLanguage: A mobile node can change its network attachment while the access network manages its mobility. This RFC explains how the network can also maintain the node's multicast group subscriptions.

sections.title: The MAG and LMA Roles
sections.content:
A mobile node sends MLD reports and done messages on its local link as if it were on a fixed network. The MAG receives these messages and runs an MLD proxy instance for the tunnel to the node's LMA. The proxy aggregates membership reports from the downstream mobile nodes and forwards the aggregate upstream.

The LMA acts as the multicast router or another MLD proxy. It uses the reports to create or update multicast forwarding state and sends subscribed multicast traffic through the tunnel to the MAG. The MAG then forwards the traffic to the relevant access links.
sections.plainLanguage: The mobile node reports which groups it wants to receive. Its MAG combines those reports and sends them to the LMA, which forwards matching multicast traffic back through the tunnel.

sections.title: Refreshing Subscriptions After a Handover
sections.content:
After a mobile node attaches to a new MAG, the MAG sends an MLD General Query on the new link to learn the node's current group memberships. The node replies with MLD reports. The MAG adds its new downstream link to the proxy instance associated with the node's LMA and reports any membership changes upstream.

The MAG maintains and aggregates the subscriptions of its attached nodes. The LMA does not need to query the tunnel after every handover. MLD timers and the Robustness Variable should be set to account for the timing of handovers and proxy configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: When the node arrives at a new gateway, the gateway asks which multicast groups it wants. The gateway updates its proxy state and tells the LMA if the subscriptions changed.

sections.title: IPv4, Multiple Interfaces, and Network Design
sections.content:
For IPv4 multicast, mobile nodes use Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) signaling, and MAGs provide IGMP proxy functions in an analogous way to MLD proxies. In a dual-stack access network, the MAG chooses signaling based on the link's address configuration; duplicate traffic may occur across IPv4 and IPv6 groups.

A mobile node may use multiple interfaces for multicast subscriptions, but this approach does not support a make-before-break handover for uninterrupted service continuation. If multicast is already available throughout an access network, other proxy or routing arrangements may be possible. The RFC says those approaches need further investigation.
sections.plainLanguage: The deployment can also support IPv4 multicast through IGMP. A device with multiple interfaces can keep separate subscriptions on them, but the RFC does not promise an uninterrupted handover between interfaces.

sections.title: Security and Resource Use
sections.content:
The document adds no new messages or protocol operations beyond the referenced mobility and multicast specifications. It warns that rapid membership changes during mobility can consume resources at PMIPv6 routers and access networks. Large multicast streams can also burden access networks with limited capacity.

Authorization checks for mobile nodes and rate controls at replicators may be needed. MAG proxy implementations should remove multicast state automatically when a mobile node leaves, because the node will not send a leave message before departure.
sections.plainLanguage: Rapid changes in subscriptions can use network resources, so the network may need authorization checks and rate controls. A gateway must also clear stale membership state when a device leaves.
